market.title: Fired general accused of being source for Wall Street Journal, NYT
market.summary: The Pentagon's former top military planner is under federal investigation and may face a court-martial for allegedly leaking to reporters from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, according to three sources familiar with the controversy. Why it matters: Former Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week after being accused of misconduct as part of the department's war on leaks. Sylvia failed four polygraphs and admitted to the incidents during two interviews on video that lasted more than a total of two hours, according to details from an internal Pentagon report shared with Axios. "The president has no tolerance for leakers, so Sylvia's termination is the first step in the accountability process, not the last," one of the sources said. Zoom in: Starting in the fall of 2025, the sources said, Sylvia gave information without authorization to reporters Michael Gordon of the Wall Street Journal and Greg Jaffe of the New York Times. Neither reporter is suspected or accused of doing anything illegal, improper or unprofessional in their reporting. Journalists often rely on confidential sources in reporting on issues that involve institutions where insiders aren't authorized to speak publicly. The report states Sylvia admitted to more extensive contacts with Gordon in 2025 and 2026, when the general allegedly shared classified information about Ukraine and Iran with the reporter. The Justice Department is investigating that. Only one discussion with Jaffe appears in the investigative report, concerning Hegseth's unexplained purging of military leaders. Sources said the unauthorized communication by Sylvia potentially violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice's prohibition of "conduct unbecoming of an officer." Behind the scenes: Sylvia allegedly admitted to first disclosing information to Gordon in the fall of 2025 when the two met in the Pentagon and discussed unspecified information about Ukraine, the sources said. After the Wall Street Journal and other outlets were barred from the Pentagon, Sylvia met Gordon at the Silver Diner in Arlington, Va., to give information about a book the reporter was planning to write, the report said. "Major General Sylvia relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally brief Gordon on assistance to Ukraine," said the report, which emphasized that Sylvia didn't receive clearance to discuss the sensitive information. A separate legal analysis of Sylvia's conduct alleged that the general also discussed "munitions stockpiles and high-level interagency discussions with Iran" that were classified, according to a source briefed on the document. Then, "sometime in June or July," Gordon sent Sylvia a message on the encrypted app Signal, the report said. "Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message" the report said. "But he believed it had something to do with Iran. He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it." While deleting the message, Sylvia allegedly told military investigators that "he believed he deleted the entire message thread with Michael Gordon. This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on [Sylvia's] personal phone." Sylvia "indicated multiple times he was comfortable with what he told Gordon about Ukraine assistance," the report said without elaborating. The intrigue: Sylvia's case has led to some friction in the Pentagon after the Joint Staff initially issued a positive statement about the general immediately after he was terminated. The Joint Staff retracted its statement after senior Defense Department officials sent word that Sylvia had been fired for allegedly leaking. A source familiar with the investigation said the Joint Staff should have known better. "You don't get four polygraphs deep without the head of the Joint Staff being briefed at some point. Why wasn't he flagged, what red flags flared up?" the source said. "Their first statement, they gave him a farewell — you know, 'We wish you well in your future endeavors' — and had to retract that information after the truth came out," the source said. "So there's a level of culpability within the Joint Staff that I think is a critical part of this they need to answer for." What they're saying: The Joint Staff declined to comment and referred questions to the Justice Department. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal declined to comment. Sylvia could not be reached for comment. The Defense Department referred Axios to a statement by Assistant Defense Secretary Sean Parnell, who said last week that "classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it."

market.title: Elon Musk's next target: A major shake-up of America's wireless market
market.summary: Elon Musk is looking to shake up America's wireless industry, potentially bringing the first major new competitive threat in years to a business dominated by three companies. Why it matters: The cellular industry has seen enormous technological change, but relatively little disruption to its competitive structure. Musk has the money, spectrum and satellite network to attempt something different — though he faces daunting obstacles. Driving the news: SpaceX is assembling the pieces to become a major U.S. wireless carrier, potentially building its own terrestrial network and buying available spectrum. The moves are meant either to build the capability to bypass existing carriers or to bring them to the table for a deal that would allow Musk to strike a deal for wholesale access to their networks. Musk may have reason to move quickly while the current administration and its regulatory appointees remain in place, a reason some analysts have cited in the context of proposals for a merger between Tesla and SpaceX . What they're saying: Blair Levin, a former FCC chief of staff who now heads policy at Optimal Advisory, says Musk's financial resources distinguish him from previous challengers. "For the first time, there is an entity capable of scaring investors in the traditional big three," Levin told Axios. Unlike Dish, which faced serious financing constraints, SpaceX can draw on capital markets that have rewarded Musk's ambitious plans. The latest : SpaceX has held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network arrangements, according to a Washington Post report Monday. That could provide a quick route to customers and infrastructure, although approval of such a deal is far from a foregone conclusion if Musk's businesses are drawn into a regulator quagmire after the midterm elections. The Post reported that Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile have all rebuffed Musk's efforts to gain access to their networks. State of play: Musk also has a path to maneuver around them. SpaceX has agreed to multibillion-dollar spectrum deals , including a low-band variety useful for reaching customers indoors and supporting a traditional cellular network. The company could build its own network using towers and smaller rooftop antennas, though doing so would require substantial investment and time. The big picture: America's wireless industry has spent much of the past two decades consolidating. T-Mobile once played the scrappy challenger, shaking up the industry with aggressive pricing and the elimination of unpopular practices. But its 2020 acquisition of Sprint reduced the number of major nationwide carriers from four to three. Regulators tried to preserve a fourth competitor by requiring the sale of Boost Mobile to Dish Network, which planned to build a nationwide network. That effort never delivered the competitive alternative envisioned, leaving Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile firmly entrenched. The intrigue: Musk would be moving from a business where SpaceX enjoys enormous technical and economic advantages to one where the established players have spent decades building infrastructure, acquiring customers and learning how to serve them. In terrestrial wireless, the big three carriers have spent decades investing in towers, spectrum, indoor coverage and the countless small improvements that make their networks reliable. Building such a network isn't simply a matter of spending billions on infrastructure, Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson said in a recent podcast interview. It also means catching up on decades of work filling in coverage gaps in stadiums, airports and other difficult locations. The catch: Even if Musk can assemble the necessary infrastructure, it's far from clear that becoming a nationwide wireless carrier would be a particularly attractive business. Moffett questions why SpaceX would want to enter an industry where even the established carriers struggle to earn attractive returns on their investments. Between the lines: Success will depend on fundamentally lowering the cost of providing service or creating something for which consumers are willing to pay extra. SpaceX has floated the idea of using Starlink rooftop equipment as small cellular base stations, potentially reducing some of the costs of building a traditional network. The political backdrop: Musk's plans come as Washington faces a potentially significant shift following Tuesday's midterm elections. While SpaceX is likely to face significant political and regulatory risks due to Musk's ties with Republicans, analysts aren't sure that will translate into opposing a wireless deal that adds competition to the market. The bottom line: Musk has repeatedly succeeded in industries where established players doubted his ambitions. But this time he's the outsider, trying to overcome the advantages of companies that have spent decades building the networks he wants to challenge.
